# Chapter 4: 4. Managing Contacts: Customers and Suppliers

## A Real‑World Situation: When Your “One‑Customer” Turns Into a Whole List

Imagine you run a boutique coffee shop called **Bean & Brew**. For the first six months you only sold coffee to walk‑in customers, and you ordered beans from a single local roaster. Your bookkeeping in Xero is simple: one sales invoice a day, one bill a week.  

Now the shop is thriving. You’ve started a **loyalty program**, you sell beans online, and you’re sourcing chocolate, milk, and pastry supplies from three new vendors. Each new customer and supplier must be recorded in Xero so that invoices, bills, and reports stay accurate.  

If you try to type every detail by hand each time a contact is added, you’ll waste time, risk errors, and lose the ability to group contacts for reporting. This chapter shows you how to **create, organize, and maintain contact records** efficiently—whether you add them one‑by‑one or import a whole list at once. By the end, you’ll be able to:

1. **Create new contact profiles** and place them in the right groups (e.g., “Retail Customers”, “Wholesale Suppliers”).  
2. **Import contacts in bulk** using a CSV file, saving hours of manual entry.  
3. **Set payment terms, tax settings, and default currencies** so every transaction defaults to the correct parameters.

Let’s dive in.

---

## 1. Adding a Single Customer or Supplier

### 1.1 Where to Find the Contacts Screen  

From the Xero dashboard (see Chapter 3), click the **“Contacts”** tab in the top navigation bar. This opens the master list where all customers and suppliers live.  

> **Tip:** If you’re using the mobile app, tap the **menu icon → Contacts**.

### 1️⃣ Step‑by‑Step: Creating a New Contact  

1. **Click “+ New Contact”** at the top right of the list.  
2. **Choose the contact type** – *Customer* or *Supplier*. Xero treats both as “contacts” but the type determines which transaction screens (Invoice vs. Bill) will pre‑select the contact.  
3. **Enter the basic details**:  
   - **Name** – the legal name or trading name.  
   - **Email** – used for automatic invoice/bill delivery.  
   - **Phone** – optional but handy for follow‑ups.  
4. **Add an address** (optional but recommended for tax reports).  
5. **Set the contact’s status**: *Active* (default) or *Archived* if you no longer deal with them.  

> **Note:** The first time you see a field like “Tax‑ID” or “Bank Account”, Xero will display a brief tooltip explaining its purpose. Keep those tooltips handy—they’re great for beginners.

### 1.2 Assigning Groups  

Groups let you filter contacts quickly, e.g., “Online Customers” or “Local Suppliers”.  

1. In the same “New Contact” window, scroll to **“Contact Groups”**.  
2. Click **“Add to Group”** and select an existing group or type a new name and hit **Enter** to create it on the fly.  

> **Best Practice:** Use **descriptive, plural names** (e.g., “Wholesale Suppliers”) so the purpose is instantly clear.

### 1.3 Setting Payment Terms, Tax Settings, and Currency  

These defaults appear whenever you create an invoice or bill for the contact.

| Field | What It Controls | Typical Values |
|-------|------------------|----------------|
| **Payment Terms** | Days before payment is due (e.g., Net 30) | Net 30, Net 15, Due On Receipt |
| **Tax Settings** | Whether the contact is taxable and which tax rate applies | Standard, Reduced, Exempt |
| **Default Currency** | Currency for transactions (useful for overseas customers) | USD, EUR, GBP, etc. |

To set them:

1. Locate the **“Payment Terms”** dropdown and choose the appropriate term.  
2. Under **“Tax Settings”**, tick **“Taxable”** if the contact should be charged tax, then pick the tax rate from the list (these rates are defined in **Settings → Tax Rates**).  
3. For **“Default Currency”**, click the currency field and select the appropriate code.  

> **Quick Check:** If you leave any of these fields blank, Xero will fall back to the organization‑wide defaults you set in Chapter 2 (“Setting Up Your Xero Organization”). That can lead to mismatched invoices, so always verify them when you first create the contact.

### 1.4 Saving the Contact  

When all fields are complete, click **“Save”.** The contact now appears in the master list, highlighted with its group tags.  

You can always edit a contact later by clicking its name, updating fields, and hitting **“Save”** again.

---

## 2. Organizing Contacts with Groups and Tracking Categories

### 2.1 Why Groups Matter  

Groups are not just visual labels; they affect reporting. For example, you can run a **Customer Sales Summary** filtered by the “Online Customers” group to see how much revenue comes from your e‑commerce channel.  

### 2.2 Creating and Managing Groups  

1. From the **Contacts** screen, click **“Manage Groups”** (gear icon).  
2. Click **“+ New Group”**, type a name, and optionally add a short description.  
3. Click **“Save”**.  

To **add existing contacts** to a group:

1. In the contact list, tick the checkboxes next to the desired contacts.  
2. Choose **“Change Group”** from the bulk‑action dropdown.  
3. Select the target group and confirm.  

### 2.3 Using Tracking Categories for Extra Detail  

Xero also offers **Tracking Categories** (found under **Settings → Tracking**) which let you tag transactions by dimensions such as “Region” or “Product Line”. While not a contact‑specific feature, you can link a contact to a tracking category by editing the contact and selecting the appropriate **“Tracking Category”** under the “Options” section.  

> **Tip:** If you anticipate needing more than one classification (e.g., both “Wholesale Supplier” and “Preferred Vendor”), use a combination of **Groups** (for static classification) and **Tracking Categories** (for dynamic reporting).

---

## 3. Importing Contacts in Bulk with CSV Files

When you have dozens or hundreds of contacts—say, after migrating from an old spreadsheet or another accounting system—entering them one‑by‑one is impractical. Xero’s **CSV import** lets you upload them all at once.

### 3.1 Preparing the CSV File  

1. **Download the template**: In the Contacts screen, click **“Import Contacts” → “Download CSV Template”**. This ensures column headings match Xero’s expectations.  
2. **Populate the template**: Fill in rows for each contact. Required columns are:  
   - **Name** (mandatory)  
   - **Contact Type** (Customer / Supplier)  
   - **Email** (optional)  
   - **Phone** (optional)  
   - **Address** (optional)  
   - **Payment Terms** (e.g., “30” for Net 30)  
   - **Taxable** (TRUE/FALSE)  
   - **Tax Rate** (exact name as defined in Xero)  
   - **Currency** (ISO code, e.g., “USD”)  
   - **Group** (comma‑separated if a contact belongs to multiple groups)  

> **Important:** Keep the **column order** exactly as in the template; otherwise Xero may misinterpret fields.

### 3.2 Running the Import  

1. In the **Contacts** screen, click **“Import Contacts”**.  
2. Choose **“Upload CSV”**, then drag‑and‑drop or browse to your prepared file.  
3. Xero will display a **preview** of the first few rows. Verify that names and email addresses appear correctly.  
4. Click **“Import”**.  

Xero processes the file and reports any **errors** (e.g., missing required fields, invalid tax rate names). Errors are listed with row numbers, allowing you to correct the CSV and re‑upload.

### 3.3 Post‑Import Clean‑Up  

After a successful import:

- **Check the Group assignments**: Go to **Contacts → Manage Groups** to confirm that the new groups were created automatically (if you used new group names).  
- **Run a quick filter**: Type a known customer name in the search bar to verify the contact appears with the correct payment terms and tax settings.  

> **Pro Tip:** If you have **duplicate contacts** (same name, different email), Xero will still import them as separate entries. Use the **“Merge Contacts”** feature (available under the contact’s dropdown menu) to combine duplicates later.

---

## 4. Setting Default Payment Terms, Tax Settings, and Currency for Multiple Contacts

Often you’ll have a whole batch of customers who share the same payment terms—say, all **“Retail Customers”** pay Net 30, while **“Wholesale Customers”** pay Net 45. Updating each contact individually is tedious, but Xero lets you apply defaults in bulk.

### 4.1 Bulk Editing via the Contact List  

1. In the **Contacts** screen, filter the list to the desired group (e.g., click the **“Retail Customers”** group tag).  
2. Tick the checkbox at the top of the list to **select all** displayed contacts.  
3. From the **bulk‑action dropdown**, choose **“Change Payment Terms”**, **“Change Tax Settings”**, or **“Change Currency”** as needed.  
4. Pick the new default value and confirm.  

All selected contacts will now inherit the chosen default.

### 4.2 Using the “Contact Settings” Page for Organization‑Wide Defaults  

If you realize that **most** of your contacts share the same payment terms, you can adjust the **organization default** so that any new contact you create automatically inherits it:

1. Navigate to **Settings → General Settings**.  
2. Under **“Default Payment Terms”**, select the preferred term (e.g., **Net 30**).  
3. Save changes.  

> **Caution:** Changing the organization default **does not retroactively update existing contacts**; it only affects new ones. Use the bulk‑edit method above for existing records.

### 4.3 Handling Multiple Tax Rates  

If you sell both **taxable** and **tax‑exempt** products, you may need separate contacts for each tax scenario. Create two groups—**“Taxable Customers”** and **“Exempt Customers”**—and assign the appropriate tax setting during bulk edit.  

When you later generate invoices, Xero will automatically pull the tax setting from the contact record, reducing the chance of charging the wrong tax rate.

---

## 5. Maintaining Clean Contact Data Over Time

A contact list can quickly become messy—old customers linger, suppliers change bank details, or duplicate entries appear. Good housekeeping ensures that your financial reports stay reliable.

### 5.1 Archiving vs. Deleting  

- **Archive**: Marks a contact as inactive but retains its historical transactions. Use this for customers who haven’t bought in a long time or suppliers you no longer use. Archived contacts are hidden from the default view but can be re‑activated if needed.  
- **Delete**: Permanently removes a contact *and* all its transaction history. Xero only allows deletion if the contact has **no transactions**.  

> **Rule of Thumb:** **Never delete** a contact that has invoices, bills, or payments attached. Archive instead.

### 5.2 Merging Duplicate Contacts  

If you discover two entries for the same customer (e.g., “John Doe” and “John D.”), follow these steps:

1. Open one of the contacts.  
2. Click the **“More”** dropdown → **“Merge Contacts”**.  
3. Search for the duplicate contact, select it, and confirm.  

Xero consolidates the transaction history under the primary contact, preserving financial integrity.

### 5.3 Regular Review Checklist  

| Frequency | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| **Weekly** | Scan new contacts for missing payment terms or tax settings. |
| **Monthly** | Run a **Contact Groups** report to identify inactive customers. |
| **Quarterly** | Export the contact list (CSV) and perform a quick spreadsheet audit for duplicates or outdated details. |
| **Year‑End** | Archive any contacts without activity in the past year to keep the list lean. |

---

## 6. Practical Example: Setting Up Bean & Brew’s New Suppliers

Let’s walk through a concrete example that ties together everything you’ve learned.

### 6.1 Scenario Overview  

Bean & Brew is adding three new suppliers:

| Supplier | Type | Payment Terms | Taxable? | Currency |
|----------|------|---------------|----------|----------|
| **CocoaCo** | Supplier | Net 45 | TRUE (Standard) | USD |
| **MilkMakers Ltd.** | Supplier | Net 30 | FALSE (Exempt) | GBP |
| **PastryPro** | Supplier | Net 15 | TRUE (Reduced) | EUR |

All three belong to a new group called **“Food Ingredients”**.

### 6.2 Step‑by‑Step Execution  

1. **Create the Group**:  
   - Contacts → Manage Groups → “+ New Group” → name: *Food Ingredients* → Save.  

2. **Add Each Supplier Individually** (use the “+ New Contact” form):  
   - **CocoaCo**:  
     - Name: CocoaCo  
     - Type: Supplier  
     - Payment Terms: Net 45 (select from dropdown)  
     - Tax Settings: Tick “Taxable”, choose “Standard” rate  
     - Currency: USD  
     - Add to Group: Food Ingredients  
     - Save.  
   - **MilkMakers Ltd.**: Follow same steps, but set **Taxable = FALSE** and **Currency = GBP**.  
   - **PastryPro**: Set **Payment Terms = Net 15**, **Tax Rate = Reduced**, **Currency = EUR**.  

3. **Verify**:  
   - Filter contacts by the *Food Ingredients* group. All three suppliers should appear, each with the correct defaults.  

4. **Bulk Update (if needed)**: Suppose later you decide all food ingredient suppliers should have **Net 30** terms.  
   - Filter by *Food Ingredients* group.  
   - Tick the top checkbox → Bulk action → “Change Payment Terms” → Net 30 → Apply.  

All three contacts now share the same payment term, while retaining their individual tax and currency settings.

### 6.3 Result  

When you later enter a **Bill** for CocoaCo, Xero will automatically:

- Populate the **Net 45** due date (based on the invoice date).  
- Apply the **Standard tax rate** to the line items.  
- Record the transaction in **USD**, converting to your base currency as per the exchange rate set in Xero.  

No manual adjustments are required—your contact setup does the heavy lifting.

# Chapter 5: 5. Recording Sales: Invoices and Credit Notes

## A Real‑World Sales Encounter  

Imagine you run a small home‑decor boutique called **Cozy Nook**. A customer walks in, selects a handcrafted lamp worth **$250**, and asks you to deliver it tomorrow. You need to:

1. Create a sales invoice that records the sale, shows the tax, and links to the customer’s contact record.  
2. Send the invoice instantly by email so the customer can approve it before delivery.  
3. After delivery, the customer spots a scratch on the base and requests a **$20** discount. You’ll need to issue a credit note that reduces the amount owed and apply it to the original invoice.

All of these steps happen in Xero, and mastering them is the core of “recording sales”. The following sections walk you through each action, from generating a standard invoice to customizing its look, delivering it, and handling credit notes.

---

## 1. Creating a Standard Sales Invoice  

### 1.1 Where to Start  

From the Xero Dashboard (see Chapter 3), click **Business → Invoices**. The **Invoices** screen lists all existing sales documents and contains the **New Invoice** button at the top right.  

> **Tip:** If you have a lot of customers, use the **Search contacts** field to pull up the right contact before you start the invoice. This leverages the contact list you built in Chapter 4.

### 1.2 Filling in the Invoice Details  

When you click **New Invoice**, Xero opens a blank invoice form. The fields you’ll complete are:

| Field | What to Enter | Why it matters |
|-------|---------------|----------------|
| **To** | Select the customer (e.g., *Jane Doe*). | Links the sale to a contact, enabling tracking of receivables. |
| **Date** | Default is today; change if you need a different invoice date. | Determines the accounting period the transaction belongs to. |
| **Due Date** | Usually 30 days from the invoice date, but you can set any term. | Controls when the amount moves from **Accounts Receivable** to **Bad Debt** if unpaid. |
| **Reference** | Optional – e.g., *Order #1234*. | Helps you locate the invoice later, especially when reconciling. |
| **Item** | Choose an inventory item (e.g., *Handcrafted Lamp*). | Pulls the sales price, tax rate, and inventory quantity automatically. |
| **Quantity** | Enter **1** (or more). | Multiplies the unit price to calculate the line total. |
| **Unit Price** | Xero fills this from the item record; you can override it if needed. | Reflects the actual selling price. |
| **Tax Rate** | Select the appropriate GST/VAT rate (e.g., **10 %**). | Ensures the correct tax amount is recorded. |
| **Description** | Add a brief note (e.g., *Delivered with free assembly*). | Provides extra context for the customer and for you. |

Xero automatically calculates the **Line Total**, **Tax**, and **Invoice Total** at the bottom of the form. Review the numbers for accuracy—this is the moment where the **debit** (Accounts Receivable) and **credit** (Sales) sides of the double‑entry system meet.

### 1.3 Saving vs. Approving  

- **Save as Draft** – The invoice stays in a “Draft” status; you can edit it later.  
- **Approve** – Moves the invoice to “Awaiting Payment” and records the transaction in the ledger.  

For a walk‑in sale like Cozy Nook’s lamp, you’ll typically **Approve** immediately so the sale is captured in your books (see Chapter 2 for the importance of timely recording).

### 1.4 Adding Attachments (Optional)  

If you have a PDF of the purchase order or a design spec, click **Attachments** and upload the file. Attachments travel with the invoice when you email it, giving the customer a complete record.

---

## 2. Customizing the Invoice Layout  

Every business wants its invoices to look professional and reflect its brand. Xero lets you tailor the layout without needing a designer.

### 2.1 Accessing the Invoice Settings  

From the **Invoices** screen, click the **Settings** gear icon (top right) → **Invoice Settings**. Here you’ll find three tabs:

1. **Branding Themes** – Store multiple layout styles.  
2. **Logo & Header** – Upload your logo, set header colours, and choose a font.  
3. **Footer** – Add payment terms, bank details, or a thank‑you note.

### 2.2 Creating a New Branding Theme  

1. Click **+ New Branding Theme**.  
2. **Name** the theme (e.g., *Cozy Nook Classic*).  
3. **Logo** – Drag‑and‑drop your PNG or SVG file.  
4. **Header Colour** – Choose a colour that matches your brand palette.  
5. **Invoice Layout** – Choose between **Standard**, **Compact**, or **Detailed**.  
   - *Standard* shows a full table with item descriptions.  
   - *Compact* reduces whitespace – useful for low‑value invoices.  
   - *Detailed* adds extra columns (e.g., **Account Code**).  

6. **Footer Text** – Add a line such as:  
   > “Thank you for supporting local artisans. Pay by bank transfer to 123‑456‑789 (BankName).”  

7. Click **Save**.  

Now, when you create a new invoice, you can select the **Branding Theme** dropdown at the top of the form to apply your custom layout. Existing drafts retain their previously chosen theme, so you can switch themes even after the invoice is saved.

### 2.3 Testing Your Layout  

Before you roll out the new design to customers, generate a **Preview**:

- Open a draft invoice.  
- Click **Preview** (near the top right).  

The preview opens in a new tab, showing exactly how the PDF will appear when emailed or printed. Verify that:

- The logo is clear and correctly positioned.  
- Colours contrast well for readability.  
- All required fields (invoice number, tax amount, total) are visible.

If anything looks off, return to **Invoice Settings** → **Branding Themes** and edit the theme. Small tweaks (e.g., increasing logo size) can be made instantly.

## 3. Sending Invoices Directly from Xero  

Once the invoice is approved, the next step is to get it into the customer’s inbox.

### 3.1 Emailing an Invoice  

1. Open the approved invoice.  
2. Click **Email** at the top of the screen.  
3. Xero auto‑populates the **To** field with the contact’s primary email address.  
4. You can edit the **Subject** line (e.g., “Your Cozy Nook Invoice – #00123”).  
5. Add a personal message in the body, such as:  

   > “Hi Jane, thanks for visiting Cozy Nook! Please find attached your invoice for the handcrafted lamp. Let me know if you have any questions.”  

6. Click **Send**.  

Xero records the email as **Sent** and attaches the PDF version of the invoice automatically. In the **History & Notes** tab of the invoice, you’ll see a timestamp of the email – useful for audit trails.

### 3.2 Exporting an Invoice  

If a customer prefers a hard copy or you need to upload the invoice to another system:

1. Open the invoice.  
2. Click **Options → Export PDF**.  

The PDF downloads to your computer, ready to be printed, attached to another email, or stored in a document management system.

### 3.3 Bulk Emailing (Batch Invoicing)  

When you have multiple invoices to send (e.g., at month‑end), Xero can email them all at once:

1. Return to **Business → Invoices**.  
2. Use the checkboxes to select multiple invoices.  
3. Click **Batch Email** at the top.  

Xero opens a dialog where you can set a common subject line and message. Each selected invoice is sent individually to its respective contact, preserving personalization.

> **Note:** Batch emailing respects each contact’s **preferred email format** (HTML vs. plain text) as defined in their contact record (Chapter 4).

---

## 4. Recording a Credit Note  

A credit note reduces the amount a customer owes. It is the opposite of an invoice: instead of **debiting** Accounts Receivable, it **credits** it, while reducing Sales revenue.

### 4.1 When to Use a Credit Note  

Typical scenarios include:

- **Returned goods** (e.g., a lamp shipped with a defect).  
- **Price adjustments** after the invoice is issued.  
- **Over‑payments** that need to be refunded or applied to a future sale.  

In our Cozy Nook example, the customer discovered a scratch and requested a $20 discount. A credit note is the clean way to document that adjustment.

### 4.2 Creating the Credit Note  

1. From the Dashboard, go to **Business → Invoices**.  
2. Locate the original invoice (e.g., **#00123**) and click its **Number** to open it.  
3. In the invoice view, select **Add Credit Note** (top right).  

Xero opens a credit note form pre‑filled with:

- **To** – The same customer.  
- **Date** – Default today; change if you want the credit effective from an earlier date.  
- **Reference** – Auto‑populated with “Credit Note for #00123”.  

Enter the line details:

| Field | What to Enter |
|-------|---------------|
| **Item** | *Handcrafted Lamp* (or leave blank and use a generic “Discount”). |
| **Quantity** | **1** |
| **Unit Price** | **-20** (negative to indicate a reduction). |
| **Tax Rate** | Same rate as the original invoice (Xero will calculate a negative tax amount). |
| **Description** | “Scratch discount – agreed reduction”. |

Xero automatically calculates a **negative tax** (e.g., -$2) and a **total credit** of **- $20** (plus tax).  

### 4.3 Applying the Credit Note to the Original Invoice  

Once the credit note is saved, you have two choices:

- **Apply automatically** – Xero will show a banner on the original invoice: *“A credit note of $22.00 is available – apply now?”* Click **Apply**. The invoice status changes from **Awaiting Payment** to **Paid** (or **Partially Paid** if the credit doesn’t cover the full amount).  
- **Leave unapplied** – Useful if you intend to apply the credit to a future invoice. The credit note stays in the **Awaiting Allocation** list under **Business → Credit Notes**.

When the credit is applied, Xero creates the corresponding double‑entry:

- **Debit** – Sales (reducing revenue).  
- **Credit** – Accounts Receivable (reducing the amount the customer owes).  

All of this appears in the **History & Notes** tab, providing a transparent audit trail.

### 4.4 Sending the Credit Note  

Just like an invoice, a credit note can be emailed:

1. Open the credit note.  
2. Click **Email**.  
3. Adjust the subject line (e.g., “Credit Note #00123‑CN1 – $20 Discount”).  
4. Add a brief note:  

   > “Hi Jane, as discussed, we’ve applied a $20 discount for the scratch on your lamp. The updated balance is attached.”  

5. Click **Send**.  

The customer receives a PDF showing the original invoice amount, the credit, and the new balance—clear, professional communication.

## 5. Tracking Invoice Statuses  

Xero visually distinguishes invoice states:

- **Draft** – Not yet approved.  
- **Awaiting Payment** – Approved, but no payment recorded.  
- **Paid** – Payment received (or credit applied).  
- **Overdue** – Past the due date with no payment.  

You can filter the **Invoices** list using the **Status** dropdown. This helps you:

- Identify which invoices need follow‑up emails.  
- Spot overdue balances for cash‑flow management.  

When a payment arrives (e.g., a bank transfer), you’ll record it in the **Bank Reconciliation** step (Chapter 7). Until then, the invoice remains in **Awaiting Payment**, and the **Accounts Receivable** balance reflects the amount still owed.

## 6. Best Practices for Sales Recording  

- **Approve invoices immediately** after confirming the sale. This ensures the transaction hits the ledger right away, supporting the “timely” principle from Chapter 2.  
- **Use consistent branding** across all invoices and credit notes; it builds credibility and reduces confusion for customers.  
- **Attach supporting documents** (quotes, purchase orders) to the invoice; they’re handy for future audits.  
- **Apply credit notes promptly** to avoid “stale” credits that could be misapplied later.  
- **Review the “Awaiting Payment” list weekly**; a quick email reminder often turns overdue invoices into paid ones.

# Chapter 6: 6. Recording Purchases: Bills and Expense Claims

## A Real‑World Situation: The Office Supplies Order

Imagine you run a small design studio. Every month you buy printer paper, ink cartridges, and occasional coffee for the team. Last week the supplier emailed you a PDF bill for $375.23, and your junior designer, Maya, spent $58.40 on a client lunch that needs to be reimbursed. Both transactions must be recorded in Xero so that:

* Your profit‑and‑loss statement shows the true cost of running the business.  
* The supplier sees a timely payment on their portal.  
* Maya gets her money back without chasing the finance team.

This chapter walks you through exactly those steps: entering a supplier bill, attaching the digital receipt, and processing an employee expense claim. By the end, you’ll be confident that every purchase—whether made by the business or an employee—has a clear audit trail in Xero.

---

## 1. Entering a Supplier Bill Manually  

### 1.1 Where to Find the “Bills” Section  

From the **Dashboard** you already explored in Chapter 3, click the **Business** menu and select **Bills to pay**. This screen lists all outstanding and paid supplier bills. The **New Bill** button sits at the top right—click it to start a manual entry.

> **Tip:** If you prefer the classic layout, you can switch to “Old Style” from the gear icon in the upper right corner. The steps are identical; only the visual arrangement changes.

### 1‑2. Filling in the Bill Header  

| Field | What to Enter | Why It Matters |
|-------|---------------|----------------|
| **From** | Choose the supplier from your **Contacts** list (created in Chapter 4). | Links the bill to the correct supplier account, enabling easy tracking of what you owe them. |
| **Date** | The date on the supplier’s invoice (e.g., 12 May 2026). | Determines the period in which the expense is recognised. |
| **Due Date** | Usually the payment terms (e.g., 30 days). Xero can auto‑calculate if you enter the **Terms** (e.g., 30 days). | Helps you manage cash flow and avoid late‑payment penalties. |
| **Reference** | Supplier invoice number (e.g., INV‑9876). | Provides a quick way to locate the original document later. |
| **Currency** | If you purchase in a foreign currency, select it here. | Xero will handle the conversion using the exchange rate you set. |

### 1‑3. Adding Line Items  

Each line represents a distinct expense category. Click **Add a new line** and fill out:

1. **Description** – Free‑text (e.g., “A4 printer paper – 10 reams”).  
2. **Account** – Choose the **expense account** that best matches the purchase (e.g., **Office Supplies**). Because you already know debits increase expense accounts, Xero will automatically debit this account when you save the bill.  
3. **Quantity** – Number of units (e.g., 10).  
4. **Unit Price** – Cost per unit (e.g., $30.00).  
5. **Tax Rate** – Select the appropriate GST/VAT option (e.g., **Standard – 10 %**). Xero calculates the tax amount automatically.

Repeat for each distinct item (e.g., “Ink cartridge – 2 units”). When you’re done, the **Subtotal**, **Tax**, and **Total** fields at the bottom will update in real time.

> **Note:** If you’re unsure which expense account to use, refer back to the chart of accounts you set up in Chapter 2. The right account ensures accurate reporting in the profit‑and‑loss statement.

### 1‑4. Saving vs. Approving  

* **Save as Draft** – Keeps the bill in the system but does not affect your accounts. Useful if you need to verify numbers or wait for a manager’s sign‑off.  
* **Approve** – Locks the bill, posts the expense to the selected account, and adds the amount to the **Bills to pay** list.  

For most small‑business workflows, you’ll **Approve** immediately after attaching the receipt (next section). If your organization uses a separate approval hierarchy, you can leave the bill as a draft and let a manager approve it later.

---

## 2. Attaching Digital Receipts to Bills  

### 2.1 Why Attachments Matter  

A digital receipt provides:

* **Evidence** for tax authorities during audits.  
* **Clarity** for anyone reviewing the transaction later (e.g., “Was that $375.23 for paper or ink?”).  
* **Convenience**—no need to hunt through email threads or physical folders.

Xero stores attachments alongside the bill, so the two are always linked.

### 2.2 Uploading a Receipt  

1. After you have entered the bill details, locate the **Attachments** pane at the bottom of the screen.  
2. Click **+ Add file** (or drag‑and‑drop).  
3. Browse to the PDF or image file on your computer, select it, and click **Open**.  
4. Xero will upload and display a thumbnail. You can add a short **Note** (e.g., “PDF invoice from OfficeSupplyCo”) to help identify it later.  

> **Pro tip:** If the supplier sent the invoice as an email attachment, you can forward the email to your Xero‑assigned email address (e.g., invoices@yourcompany.xero.com). Xero will automatically create a draft bill and attach the file.

### 2.3 Verifying the Attachment  

Open the attachment by clicking its thumbnail. Confirm that:

* The document is **readable** (no blurred text).  
* The **total amount** matches the bill total you entered.  
* The **date** on the document aligns with the bill’s date field.

If anything looks off, edit the bill before approving. Once approved, the attachment becomes part of the official record and cannot be altered without creating a new version.

### 2.4 Managing Multiple Attachments  

Sometimes a purchase involves several receipts (e.g., a purchase order plus a delivery note). Xero allows **multiple files** per bill. Simply repeat the upload steps for each file. The attachments will appear in chronological order, making it easy to locate the right document later.

---

## 3. Creating an Expense Claim for Employee Reimbursements  

### 3.1 When to Use an Expense Claim  

An **expense claim** is the Xero tool for tracking costs incurred by staff that the business will reimburse. Typical examples:

* Travel mileage  
* Client meals  
* Small office supplies bought with a personal credit card  

Expense claims differ from supplier bills because they are **employee‑originated** and often need a separate approval workflow.

### 3.2 Accessing the Expense Claim Interface  

1. From the **Dashboard**, click **Business** → **Expense claims**.  
2. Click **New expense claim** (top right).  

You’ll see a form similar to the bill entry screen, but with a few extra fields tailored to employee reimbursements.

### 3‑3. Populating the Claim Form  

| Field | What to Enter | Guidance |
|-------|---------------|----------|
| **Employee** | Choose the staff member who incurred the expense (e.g., **Maya Patel**). | Xero pulls the employee’s contact details from the **Contacts** list. |
| **Date** | Date the expense was incurred (e.g., 14 May 2026). | This date determines the accounting period for the expense. |
| **Reference** | Optional – could be a receipt number or internal note. | Helpful for later searches. |
| **Description** | General description (e.g., “Client lunch with XYZ Corp”). | Provides context for the approver. |
| **Currency** | Usually your base currency, unless the expense was overseas. | Xero will convert automatically if needed. |

#### Adding Line Items  

1. Click **Add a new line**.  
2. **Account** – Select the appropriate expense account (e.g., **Meals & Entertainment**).  
3. **Amount** – Enter the net amount (excluding tax). Xero will calculate GST/VAT based on the **Tax Rate** you choose.  
4. **Tax Rate** – Choose the correct rate (e.g., **Standard – 10 %**).  

If the expense includes multiple categories (e.g., “Taxi fare” and “Parking”), add a separate line for each.

### 3‑4. Attaching the Employee’s Receipt  

Just like with supplier bills, scroll to the **Attachments** section and upload the scanned receipt or photo Maya took on her phone. Encourage employees to:

* Use a **clear, high‑resolution photo**.  
* Include **both sides** of the receipt if relevant.  
* Rename the file to something meaningful (e.g., “Maya‑Lunch‑2026‑05‑14.jpg”).

### 3‑5. Submitting the Claim for Approval  

Once all lines and attachments are in place, click **Submit**. The claim now appears in the **Submitted** tab of the Expense Claims list. Depending on your organization’s settings (configured in **Settings → General Settings → Expense Claims**), the claim will:

* **Notify** the designated approver via email.  
* **Remain editable** only by the employee until an approver takes action.  

### 3‑6. Approving and Paying the Claim  

An approver (often a manager or the business owner) opens the claim, reviews the details, and clicks **Approve**. Xero then:

* **Posts** the expense amounts to the selected accounts.  
* **Creates a payable** in the **Bills to pay** list, linked to the employee’s contact.  

To reimburse Maya, you can either:

* **Pay the bill** directly from the **Bills to pay** screen using your bank feed (covered later in Chapter 7).  
* **Record a manual payment** (e.g., cash or a personal check) by clicking **Mark as Paid** and entering the payment method.  

After payment, Xero automatically marks the claim as **Paid** and updates the employee’s reimbursement status.

> **Best practice:** Keep a consistent naming convention for expense claim attachments (e.g., *Employee‑Date‑Purpose*). This habit speeds up future audits and reduces the chance of misplaced receipts.

## 4. Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them  

| Pitfall | Why It Happens | Quick Fix |
|---------|----------------|-----------|
| **Forgetting to attach the receipt** | Busy moments; assumption that the PDF is already linked. | Make attachment the **last step** before saving/approving, and use the “Submit” button as a mental cue. |
| **Choosing the wrong expense account** | Confusion between similar accounts (e.g., “Office Supplies” vs. “Stationery”). | Refer to the chart of accounts (Chapter 2) and, if still unsure, ask your accountant. |

# Chapter 7: 7. Bank Feeds and Reconciliation

## A Real‑World Wake‑Up Call  

Sarah runs a boutique coffee shop called “Bean There.” Every month she receives a PDF bank statement with dozens of line items: cash sales, credit‑card fees, a loan repayment, and a vendor invoice she paid by check. She manually types each transaction into Xero, then spends another hour scrolling through the bank reconciliation screen trying to line everything up. At the end of the month she still sees a handful of “unreconciled” items and wonders whether she missed something.  

Sarah’s problem is common: **bank feeds and reconciliation are the bridge between the bank’s record and the accounting records you keep in Xero.** When the bridge is built correctly, transactions appear automatically, matching is fast, and unreconciled items disappear. The steps below show exactly how to create that bridge, import data when a feed isn’t possible, and keep the reconciliation process clean and reliable.

## Understanding the Two Paths to Xero  

### What Is a Bank Feed?  

A **bank feed** is an electronic connection between your bank (or credit‑card provider) and Xero. Once the connection is authorized, the bank pushes daily transaction data directly into the **Bank Accounts** tab of Xero. The feed eliminates the need to download, format, or manually upload statements.

*Advantages*  

- Automatic daily updates  
- Real‑time visibility of cash flow  
- Fewer data‑entry errors  

*Limitations*  

- Not all banks support feeds (especially smaller regional banks)  
- Initial setup may require a bank‑portal login or a third‑party service (e.g., Yodlee)  

### What Is a Bank Statement File?  

When a feed isn’t available, you can **import a bank statement file**. Xero accepts several file formats—**CSV**, **OFX**, **QIF**, and **QBO**—each containing a list of transactions with date, description, and amount. The file is uploaded once (or each month) and the transactions are added to the same Bank Accounts screen.

*Key point*: Whether the data arrives via feed or file, the next step is **bank reconciliation**, where each line is matched to an invoice, bill, or other transaction recorded in Xero.

## Setting Up a Bank Feed  

1. **Navigate to the Bank Accounts page**  
   - From the Xero Dashboard, click **Accounting** → **Bank accounts**.  
2. **Add a new bank account**  
   - Click **Add Bank Account** (top right).  
   - Search for your bank’s name. Xero lists the banks that support a feed.  
3. **Choose the feed type**  
   - **Direct feed** – you’ll be redirected to your bank’s login page.  
   - **Yodlee feed** – you’ll log in through a third‑party aggregator that securely stores your credentials.  
4. **Enter your banking credentials**  
   - Follow the on‑screen prompts. Most banks ask for your online banking username, password, and possibly a security question or OTP (one‑time password).  
5. **Select the account(s) to connect**  
   - If you have multiple accounts (e.g., checking and savings), tick the ones you want to feed into Xero.  
6. **Set the start date**  
   - Choose the date from which you want transactions imported. Picking a date after your last manual entry avoids duplicate lines.  
7. **Confirm and finish**  
   - Xero will display a “Connected” status and begin pulling the most recent transactions.  

> **Tip**: Keep a record of the bank login you used for the feed. If the bank changes its security policy, you’ll need to re‑authorize the connection.

## Importing a Bank Statement File  

If your bank does not support a feed, follow these steps each month (or whenever you receive a statement):

1. **Download the statement in a supported format**  
   - Log in to your bank portal, locate the “download statement” option, and select **CSV** (recommended) or OFX/QIF.  
2. **Prepare the file**  
   - Ensure the file includes the required columns: **Date**, **Description**, **Amount** (positive for deposits, negative for withdrawals).  
   - Xero’s CSV template can be used as a reference; you can copy your data into that template if your bank’s export uses different headings.  
3. **Upload the file**  
   - In Xero, go to **Accounting** → **Bank accounts**, select the relevant bank account, then click **Import a Statement**.  
   - Drag the file onto the upload area or browse to locate it.  
4. **Map the columns (if prompted)**  
   - Xero may ask you to confirm which column represents the date, description, and amount. Adjust as needed.  
5. **Review the imported transactions**  
   - Xero will show a preview; confirm that the amounts and dates look correct, then click **Import**.  

> **Note**: After a file import, Xero marks the imported rows as **“Imported”** but not yet reconciled. They will appear on the Reconciliation screen ready for matching.

## The Reconciliation Dashboard  

Once transactions are in Xero—whether via feed or file—you’ll work in the **Reconcile** view:

- **Left pane**: List of **unreconciled bank lines** (newly imported transactions).  
- **Right pane**: List of **open transactions** in Xero (e.g., unpaid invoices, outstanding bills).  

The goal is to pair each line from the left with a corresponding line on the right, or to create a new entry if none exists.

### Visual cues  

- **Green tick** – transaction already reconciled.  
- **Blue “Match” suggestion** – Xero’s automatic guess based on amount, date, and contact.  
- **Red “Unmatched”** – no suggestion; you’ll need to act manually.  

## Matching Transactions to Existing Records  

### Automatic matching  

When the amount and date of a bank line closely align with an open invoice or bill, Xero will show a **Match** button. To accept:

1. Click **Match**.  
2. Review the suggested invoice/bill.  
3. Click **OK** to confirm.  

Xero will automatically create the double‑entry: debit **Bank** (increase) and credit **Sales** or **Accounts Payable**, depending on the source document. This follows the double‑entry principle introduced earlier.

### Manual matching with “Find & Match”  

If no automatic suggestion appears, you can search:

1. Select the bank line.  
2. Click **Find & Match**.  
3. Use the filter box to search by contact name, invoice number, or amount.  
4. Tick the correct transaction(s) and click **Match**.  

### Creating a Spend Money transaction  

Sometimes a bank line represents a payment that has **no corresponding bill**—for example, a utility bill you paid before entering the bill into Xero. In that case:

1. Click the bank line.  
2. Choose **Create** → **Spend Money**.  
3. Xero will pre‑fill the **Bank** account (the one you’re reconciling) and the **Amount**.  
4. Select the appropriate **Expense Account** (e.g., *Utilities*).  
5. Add a description and, if desired, attach a receipt.  
6. Click **Save**.  

The transaction is now recorded with a debit to the expense account and a credit to the bank account, keeping the accounting equation balanced.

### Creating a Receive Money transaction  

If the bank line is a customer payment not yet linked to an invoice:

1. Click the line, then **Create** → **Receive Money**.  
2. Choose the **Customer** and the **Invoice** (or leave blank if it’s an advance).  
3. Confirm the amount and click **Save**.  

## Resolving Unreconciled Items  

Even with a solid feed, a few items may remain unreconciled. Common reasons include:

- **Timing differences**: A payment recorded in Xero on the 31st may not appear on the bank statement until the 2nd of the next month.  
- **Bank fees**: Service charges often appear as a small debit with a description like “Monthly Service Fee.”  
- **Duplicate imports**: If you imported a statement covering a period already fed, the same transaction appears twice.  

### Step‑by‑step investigation  

1. **Identify the line** – note the date, description, and amount.  
2. **Search Xero** – use the global search (top‑right magnifying glass) with the amount or a keyword from the description.  
3. **Check the date range** – if the transaction falls outside the period you’ve already reconciled, consider it a timing issue; you can hold it for the next month’s reconciliation.  
4. **Create a missing entry** – if the transaction truly has no counterpart, use **Spend Money** or **Receive Money** as appropriate.  
5. **Delete a duplicate** – if you find an identical entry already reconciled, click the bank line, select **Options** → **Delete**.  

### Marking items as reconciled without a match  

In rare cases you may need to **“Mark as Reconciled”** manually (e.g., a bank error). Use this sparingly, and always add a note explaining why you took this step; the note will appear in the reconciliation reports.

## Understanding Reconciliation Reports  

Xero provides two primary reports that let you verify that your bank reconciliation is complete and accurate.

### Bank Reconciliation Summary  

- **Location**: Accounting → Reports → Bank Reconciliation Summary.  
- **What it shows**: For each bank account, the report lists the **opening balance**, **total reconciled amount**, **total unreconciled amount**, and **closing balance**.  
- **Why it matters**: The closing balance should match the balance shown on your bank statement. Any variance signals an issue that needs investigation.  

### Bank Reconciliation Detail  

- **Location**: Accounting → Reports → Bank Reconciliation Detail.  
- **What it shows**: A line‑by‑line view of every bank transaction, indicating whether it is **reconciled** (with a link to the source document) or **unreconciled**.  
- **Why it matters**: Use this report to audit the matching process, verify that each invoice and bill has been correctly linked, and to provide evidence for auditors or tax authorities.  

Both reports can be exported as PDF or CSV for record‑keeping.

## Tips for a Smooth Reconciliation Routine  

- **Reconcile daily**: The smaller the batch, the easier it is to spot mismatches.  
- **Use consistent naming**: When you create invoices or bills, include the same wording that appears on the bank statement (e.g., “ABC Supplies – Invoice 1023”). This improves Xero’s automatic matching.  
- **Watch for fees and interest**: Create a dedicated **Bank Fees** expense account to capture these items; they’ll appear as unreconciled lines until you record them.  
- **Avoid duplicate imports**: After a feed is active, turn off manual imports for the same period.  
- **Leverage the “Rules” feature** (found under **Accounting → Bank accounts → Bank Rules**) to auto‑categorise recurring transactions, such as weekly rent payments.  

## Common Pitfalls and How to Fix Them  

| Pitfall | Symptom | Fix |
|---------|---------|-----|
| **Duplicate transactions** | Same amount appears twice, one marked “Imported,” the other “Feed.” | Delete the duplicate or use the “Mark as Reconciled” option after confirming the correct entry. |
| **Unmatched payments** | Bank line shows a credit, but no open invoice matches. | Create a **Receive Money** transaction, then apply the payment to the appropriate invoice later. |
| **Unreconciled fees** | Small negative amounts with generic descriptions remain unreconciled. | Record a **Spend Money** transaction to a **Bank Fees** expense account, then reconcile. |
| **Timing gaps** | A transaction dated 31 Dec appears on the statement on 2 Jan, leaving a gap at month‑end. | Leave the line unreconciled until the next month’s feed or import, then reconcile. |
| **Incorrect account mapping** | Imported CSV columns are mis‑matched, causing dates or amounts to shift. | Re‑import the file after correcting the column mapping; Xero will replace the previous import for that period. |

## Automating the Process with Bank Rules  

For recurring transactions (e.g., a weekly payroll payment), you can set up a **Bank Rule**:

1. Go to **Accounting** → **Bank accounts**, click the bank account, then **Bank Rules**.  
2. Click **Add Rule** and define criteria (e.g., **Description contains “Payroll”**).  
3. Choose the **Transaction Type** (Spend Money) and the **Account** (e.g., *Salaries Expense*).  
4. Save the rule.  

From then on, any new bank line meeting the criteria will be automatically categorized and ready for reconciliation, reducing manual effort dramatically.

## Summary Workflow  

1. **Connect** a bank feed **or** **import** a statement file.  
2. **Review** the Reconciliation screen each day.  
3. **Accept** automatic matches, or use **Find & Match**, **Spend Money**, and **Receive Money** to create the missing link.  
4. **Investigate** any unreconciled items, correcting timing, fees, or duplicates.  
5. **Run** the Bank Reconciliation Summary and Detail reports monthly to confirm that the Xero bank balance equals the bank statement balance.  

By following this repeatable process, the bank account in Xero becomes a reliable, real‑time reflection of your actual cash, and you can trust the financial reports you’ll generate later in the course.

## Key Takeaways  

- A **bank feed** pulls daily transactions automatically; a **bank statement file** is a manual upload for banks that don’t support feeds.  
- Set up a feed via **Accounting → Bank accounts → Add Bank Account**, or import a CSV/OFX/QIF file when required.  
- The **Reconcile** screen pairs bank lines with existing invoices, bills, or creates **Spend Money/Receive Money** entries when no match exists.  
- Unreconciled items arise from timing differences, fees, or duplicate imports; resolve them by searching, creating missing entries, or deleting duplicates.  
- Use the **Bank Reconciliation Summary** and **Detail** reports to verify that Xero’s bank balance matches the actual statement balance.  
- Daily reconciliation, consistent naming, and automated **Bank Rules** keep the process efficient and error‑free.

# Chapter 8: 8. Managing Expenses and Fixed Assets

## A Real‑World Snapshot  

Imagine **BrightIdeas Consulting**, a two‑person start‑up that just landed a $5,000 project. Within the first week, the founder books a flight to meet the client, a junior analyst submits a receipt for a coffee‑shop lunch, and the company buys a new high‑spec laptop for design work.  

Each of these costs must be:

* **Categorised** so the profit‑and‑loss statement shows exactly where money is being spent.  
* **Tracked** against a cost centre (e.g., “Client‑Travel” vs. “Office‑Equipment”) so the founder can see the true cost of winning the project.  
* **Recorded correctly** in Xero so that the bank feed, the trial balance, and future depreciation all line up.

The steps you’ll follow in this chapter turn that jumble of receipts into clean, audit‑ready data—all without leaving Xero.

---

## Expense Categorisation and Cost Centres  

### What Is an Expense Account?  

In the double‑entry system you explored earlier, every transaction touches **two accounts**: one is debited, the other credited. An *expense account* is a **debit‑type** account that records the outflow of resources used to generate revenue (e.g., *Travel Expenses*, *Office Supplies*, *Software Subscriptions*). When you record an expense, the expense account is **debited**, and the offsetting account (usually *Bank* or *Accounts Payable*) is **credited**.

### Why Use Cost Centres?  

A **cost centre** (called a *tracking category* in Xero) is a label that lets you slice expenses by project, department, location, or any other dimension that matters to your business. Cost centres do **not** create separate accounts; they simply add a second layer of reporting.  

*Example*: The same *Travel Expenses* account can be split into “Client‑Travel” and “Team‑Training” cost centres, letting you compare how much you spend on each activity without cluttering the Chart of Accounts.

### Setting Up Tracking Categories in Xero  

1. **Navigate** → *Settings* → *Tracking*.  
2. Click **Add Tracking Category**.  
3. Give it a clear name (e.g., **Project**).  
4. Add **options** (e.g., *BrightIdeas‑001*, *BrightIdeas‑002*, *Internal*).  

> **Tip** – Keep the list short and meaningful; too many options become hard to maintain.

Once created, any expense entry can be tagged with a tracking option, instantly feeding cost‑centre reports.

### Assigning an Expense to the Right Account and Cost Centre  

When you enter a bill or a spend‑money transaction, Xero asks for:

| Field | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| **Account** | Choose the appropriate expense account from the Chart of Accounts. |
| **Tracking** | Select the relevant cost‑centre option you just set up. |
| **Amount** | Enter the monetary value. |
| **Description** | Add a brief note for future reference. |

The combination of *Account + Tracking* tells Xero **where** the money went **and why**.

---

## Recording Everyday Expenses  

### 1. Bills vs. Spend Money vs. Expense Claims  

| Transaction Type | When to Use | Typical Source |
|------------------|-------------|----------------|
| **Bills** | Supplier invoices that you’ll pay later (credit terms). | Paper or emailed invoices. |
| **Spend Money** | Direct cash or bank payments that don’t have an invoice (e.g., petty cash, online purchases). | Credit‑card receipts, cash‑out slips. |
| **Expense Claims** | Costs incurred by employees that need reimbursement. | Employee‑submitted receipts. |

All three routes flow through the same underlying double‑entry logic, but Xero provides specialised screens to make data entry faster and to keep audit trails clear.

### 2. Step‑by‑Step: Entering a Bill for Office Supplies  

1. **Dashboard → Business → Bills to Pay** → *New Bill*.  
2. **Supplier**: Choose the supplier you previously added (see Chapter 4).  
3. **Date**: Invoice date.  
4. **Due Date**: Payment terms (e.g., 30 days).  
5. **Item Table**:  
   * **Account** → *Office Supplies* (expense).  
   * **Tracking** → *Project → Internal*.  
   * **Quantity / Unit Price** → Fill as appropriate.  
6. **Attach** the scanned receipt (drag‑and‑drop).  
7. **Approve** → Xero creates a *Bills Payable* entry that will sit in the *Accounts Payable* ledger until you reconcile it with the bank feed (Chapter 7).

### 3. Step‑by‑Step: Recording a Direct Purchase with Spend Money  

1. **Dashboard → Business → Spend Money** → *New Spend Money*.  
2. **Bank Account**: Choose the bank account (or credit card) that the money left.  
3. **To**: Select the supplier or “Cash”.  
4. **Account**: Pick the expense account (e.g., *Software Subscriptions*).  
5. **Tracking**: Tag the appropriate cost centre (e.g., *Project → BrightIdeas‑001*).  
6. **Amount**: Enter the total.  
7. **Attach** the receipt.  
8. **Save** → The transaction instantly debits the expense account and credits the chosen bank account.

Both processes generate a **source document** that will later match a bank feed line, ensuring the reconciliation you performed in Chapter 7 remains smooth.

---

## Employee Expense Claims  

### Why Use the Expense Claims Feature?  

* Employees can submit receipts from their phones.  
* Claims are automatically routed for approval.  
* Once approved, Xero creates the underlying journal entry, linking the expense to the correct account and cost centre.

### The Claim Lifecycle  

1. **Submission** – Employee logs into Xero (or the Xero Expenses mobile app), clicks **New Claim**, uploads a receipt, selects an expense account, adds a tracking category, and adds a brief description.  
2. **Review** – A manager (or the business owner) reviews the claim, adds notes if needed, and either **Approve** or **Reject**.  
3. **Payment** – When the claim is approved, you can either reimburse the employee via a bank transfer or a credit‑card payment. Xero creates a *Spend Money* transaction automatically, pulling the approved amount, account, and tracking data.  

### Walk‑through: Travel Claim from the Junior Analyst  

| Step | Action | Screenshot Cue (if you were looking at Xero) |
|------|--------|----------------------------------------------|
| 1 | Analyst clicks **Business → Expense Claims → New Claim**. | “+ New Claim” button at top right. |
| 2 | Uploads a PDF of the airline ticket, selects **Travel Expenses** account, tags **Project → BrightIdeas‑001**, and adds “Client meeting in New York”. | Drop‑zone for attachments, drop‑down for account, tracking selector. |
| 3 | Clicks **Submit**. | Large **Submit** button. |
| 4 | Owner receives a notification, opens the claim, checks the receipt, and clicks **Approve**. | “Approve” button on claim details page. |
| 5 | Xero automatically posts a *Spend Money* line: **Debit Travel Expenses**, **Credit Bank**. | Transaction appears in *Spend Money* list under the same claim. |
| 6 | When the bank feed shows the reimbursement (e.g., a ACH transfer to the employee), you **Match** it to the *Spend Money* line, completing the reconciliation loop. | Bank feed match screen (Chapter 7). |

**Result** – The expense is now fully recorded, cost‑centred, and reconciled, ready for reporting.

## Fixed‑Asset Management in Xero  

### What Is a Fixed Asset?  

A **fixed asset** (also called a *capital asset*) is a long‑term resource that provides economic benefit for more than one accounting period—think computers, furniture, vehicles, or leasehold improvements. Unlike consumable expenses, a fixed asset’s cost is **capitalised** and then **depreciated** over its useful life.

### The Asset Register  

Xero’s **Asset Register** lives under *Accounting → Fixed Assets*. It stores:

* Asset description  
* Purchase price  
* Date acquired  
* Depreciation method (straight‑line, diminishing‑balance, etc.)  
* Useful life (in months or years)  

All depreciation calculations are performed automatically each month, creating journal entries that hit the *Depreciation Expense* account and reduce the *Accumulated Depreciation* contra‑asset account.

### Setting Up an Asset Type  

1. **Settings → Fixed Assets → Asset Types**.  
2. Click **Add Asset Type**.  
3. Fill in:  
   * **Name** – e.g., *Computer Equipment*.  
   * **Account** – the expense account that will receive depreciation (usually *Depreciation Expense – Computer Equipment*).  
   * **Depreciation Method** – most beginners start with **Straight‑Line**.  
   * **Useful Life** – e.g., *3 years*.  
4. **Save**.  

> **Straight‑Line** spreads the cost evenly:  
> \[
> \text{Monthly Depreciation} = \frac{\text{Cost}}{\text{Useful life in months}}
> \]

### Recording a Fixed‑Asset Purchase  

Continuing the BrightIdeas scenario, the firm buys a **$2,500 MacBook Pro** on 15 May 2026.

1. **Dashboard → Accounting → Fixed Assets → New Asset**.  
2. **Asset Name** – *MacBook Pro – Serial #XYZ*.  
3. **Asset Type** – *Computer Equipment* (the type you created).  
4. **Purchase Date** – 15 May 2026.  
5. **Purchase Price** – $2,500.  
6. **Tracking** – *Project → BrightIdeas‑001* (so you can see depreciation by project).  
7. **Attach** the supplier invoice (already entered as a *Bill*).  
8. **Save**.  

Xero now creates a **journal entry**:

| Account | Debit | Credit |
|---------|-------|--------|
| **Computer Equipment (Asset)** | $2,500 | |
| **Accounts Payable** | | $2,500 |

When you later **Pay** the bill (via the bank feed), the *Accounts Payable* credit will be cleared, leaving the asset sitting on the balance sheet.

### Depreciation in Action  

On the first day of the following month (1 June 2026), Xero automatically posts the depreciation entry:

| Account | Debit | Credit |
|---------|-------|--------|
| **Depreciation Expense – Computer Equipment** | $69.44* | |
| **Accumulated Depreciation – Computer Equipment** | | $69.44* |

\*Calculation: $2,500 ÷ 36 months = $69.44 per month.

These entries appear in the *Journal* list and affect the **Profit & Loss** (through the expense) and the **Balance Sheet** (through the contra‑asset). The process repeats each month until the asset is fully depreciated or you dispose of it.

### Disposing of an Asset  

If the MacBook is sold for $800 on 31 December 2027:

1. **Create a *Fixed Asset Disposal* transaction** (Accounting → Fixed Assets → Dispose).  
2. Enter **Sale Proceeds** ($800) and the **Date**.  
3. Xero automatically posts a journal that:  

   * Removes the asset’s remaining book value.  
   * Recognises any **gain/loss** on disposal (difference between sale proceeds and net book value).  

The disposal entry ensures the asset balance returns to zero and the gain/loss shows up in the profit‑and‑loss report.

---

## Linking Expenses & Fixed Assets to Bank Reconciliation  

Every expense or asset purchase you record will eventually surface in the **Bank Feed** (Chapter 7). The reconciliation workflow remains the same:

* **Match** the bank line to the *Bill*, *Spend Money*, or *Expense Claim* you created.  
* For a fixed‑asset purchase, the match clears the *Accounts Payable* side, leaving the asset on the balance sheet.  
* Depreciation entries are **automatic**—they never appear in the bank feed because they are internal journal entries.

A quick sanity check after reconciling a month’s bank feed:

1. Run **Reports → Account Transactions** for the *Bank* account.  
2. Verify that the total of matched lines equals the bank statement balance.  
3. Run **Reports → Fixed Asset Summary** to confirm that the *MacBook* still shows a net book value of $2,500 – ($69.44 × months elapsed) = $1,? (exact figure).  

If numbers don’t line up, you’ve likely missed a matching step or entered the wrong amount—both are easy to spot with Xero’s visual reconciliation screen.

---

## Best Practices for Clean Expense & Asset Records  

| Practice | Why It Matters |
|----------|----------------|
| **Use Consistent Naming** for expense accounts and tracking categories. | Reduces search time and prevents duplicate accounts. |
| **Attach Source Documents** (receipts, invoices) at entry time. | Provides an audit trail and speeds up future reviews. |
| **Review the Asset Register Quarterly**. | Ensures useful lives and depreciation methods remain appropriate. |
| **Separate Personal vs. Business Costs**. | Keeps the trial balance clean and simplifies tax reporting later. |
| **Leverage Xero’s Mobile App** for expense claims. | Employees can submit receipts instantly, reducing lag. |
| **Set Up Automatic Reminders** for pending expense claims. | Prevents forgotten reimbursements and improves cash‑flow forecasting. |
| **Run the “Tracking Category Summary” Report** monthly. | Gives immediate insight into cost‑centre performance. |

**Common Pitfalls to Avoid**

* **Assigning an expense to the wrong account** – e.g., posting a laptop purchase to *Office Supplies* instead of capitalising it. The result is overstated expenses and missing depreciation.  
* **Neglecting tracking categories** – Without cost‑centre tags, you lose the ability to analyse project profitability.  
* **Manually entering depreciation** – Doing it by hand defeats Xero’s automation and raises the risk of errors.  
* **Skipping the attachment** – Missing receipts can cause audit headaches or tax authority queries.

## Key Takeaways  

* **Expense accounts** capture the nature of a cost; **tracking categories** (cost centres) capture *why* the cost was incurred.  
* **Bills**, **Spend Money**, and **Expense Claims** are three Xero pathways for recording expenses—choose the one that matches the source document.

# Chapter 9: 9. Generating Financial Reports

## A Real‑World Moment: Jane’s First Investor Update  

Jane runs a small graphic‑design studio that she started two years ago. After landing a new client, she needs to show the business’s health to a potential investor by the end of the month. She opens Xero, pulls the latest **Profit & Loss (P&L) statement**, checks the **Balance Sheet**, reviews the **Cash Flow Statement**, and extracts the **Aged Receivables** and **Aged Payables** reports. With a few clicks she exports everything to PDF, attaches the files to an email, and sends the package to the investor—confident that the numbers are accurate, up‑to‑date, and presented professionally.

If you’ve ever faced a similar need—whether for a loan application, a board meeting, or simply to understand how the business is performing—this chapter will walk you through generating those core financial reports in Xero, interpreting what they tell you, and sharing them with stakeholders.

---

## 1. Running the Profit & Loss Statement  

The Profit & Loss (also called the **Income Statement**) shows whether the business made a profit or a loss over a selected period. It summarises **revenues** (sales) and **expenses** (costs) to calculate **Net Profit**.

### 1.1 Where to Find the P&L  

1. From the **Dashboard**, click **Reports** in the top navigation bar.  
2. In the left‑hand list, select **Profit & Loss**.  

*(If you cannot see the Reports tab, verify that you have **Standard** or **Premium** access, as described in Chapter 3.)*

### 1.2 Choosing the Reporting Period  

Xero lets you run the P&L for any date range:

- **Pre‑set periods**: Today, This month, This quarter, This year, Last year.  
- **Custom dates**: Click the calendar icon, pick the start and end dates, then **Update**.

> **Tip:** For monthly cash‑flow monitoring, run the report for the **last 30 days**. For annual tax preparation, use the **financial year** (e.g., 1 July 2025 – 30 June 2026).

### 1.3 Understanding the Layout  

| Section | What It Shows | How It Relates to the Accounting Equation |
|---------|---------------|-------------------------------------------|
| **Revenue** | Total sales, fees, and other income | Increases **Equity** (Retained Earnings) |
| **Cost of Goods Sold (COGS)** | Direct costs of delivering services or products | Decreases **Equity** (expenses) |
| **Gross Profit** | Revenue – COGS | Indicates profitability before operating expenses |
| **Operating Expenses** | Rent, utilities, salaries, marketing, etc. | Further decreases **Equity** |
| **Net Profit (or Loss)** | Bottom line after all income and expenses | Final change to **Equity** for the period |

The **Net Profit** figure is the same number that will flow into the **Balance Sheet** under **Retained Earnings**.

### 1.4 Customising the Report  

- **Columns**: Add a **Comparative** column (e.g., current month vs. same month last year) by checking **Compare Period**.  
- **Filters**: Click **Filters** to include or exclude specific **tracking categories** (e.g., “Project A”).  
- **Display Options**: Toggle **Show Sub‑totals** for each expense group if you want more detail.

### 1.5 Saving a Snapshot  

After you have the period and layout you like:

1. Click **Save as** at the top right.  
2. Give the report a name (e.g., “P&L – June 2026”).  
3. Click **Save**.  

You can now return to this exact view with one click, useful for regular reporting cycles.

---

## 2. Generating the Balance Sheet  

The Balance Sheet provides a snapshot of the business’s **financial position** at a specific date. It lists **Assets**, **Liabilities**, and **Equity** and must always satisfy the fundamental **accounting equation**:

> **Assets = Liabilities + Equity**

### 2.1 Accessing the Balance Sheet  

1. From **Reports**, choose **Balance Sheet**.  
2. The default view shows the latest **financial year‑end** date; adjust using the calendar icon if needed.

### 2.2 Choosing a Date  

Unlike the P&L, the Balance Sheet is a **point‑in‑time** report. Common choices:

- **End of month** (e.g., 31 May 2026) for monthly reviews.  
- **Quarter‑end** (e.g., 30 September 2025) for board meetings.  
- **Year‑end** for tax filing.

### 2.3 Interpreting the Sections  

| Section | Typical Accounts | What It Means |
|---------|------------------|---------------|
| **Current Assets** | Cash, Bank accounts, Accounts Receivable, Inventory | Resources expected to be turned into cash within 12 months. |
| **Non‑Current Assets** | Fixed assets (equipment, vehicles), Intangible assets, Accumulated depreciation | Long‑term resources that support operations over several years. |
| **Current Liabilities** | Accounts Payable, Short‑term loans, GST/VAT payable | Obligations due within 12 months. |
| **Non‑Current Liabilities** | Long‑term loans, Mortgage, Deferred tax | Obligations that extend beyond one year. |
| **Equity** | Share capital, Retained earnings, Net profit for the period | Owner’s residual interest in the business. |

When the report is generated, Xero automatically pulls the balances from the **Chart of Accounts** you set up in Chapter 2. If you notice any unexpected figures, double‑check the underlying transactions (e.g., a missed invoice or an unrecorded expense) using the **Search** function.

### 2.4 Adding Comparative Columns  

To see trends, enable **Comparative** columns:

1. Click **Compare Period**.  
2. Choose a prior date (e.g., “Same date last year”).  
3. Click **Update**.

Now you can instantly see whether assets grew, liabilities shrank, or equity improved.

### 2.5 Exporting the Balance Sheet  

When you’re ready to share:

1. Click **Export** (top right).  
2. Choose **PDF** for a printable version, or **Excel** for further manipulation.  
3. Save the file to a folder you can easily locate (e.g., “Financial Reports / 2026 Quarter 2”).

## 3. Interpreting the Cash Flow Statement  

While the P&L tells you profitability, the **Cash Flow Statement** shows actual cash moving **in** and **out** of the business. Xero derives this report from the same data you’ve already entered (invoices, bills, bank feeds, etc.), applying the **indirect method**.

### 3.1 Locating the Cash Flow Report  

1. Click **Reports** → **Cash Flow**.  
2. Choose **Standard** (the default) to see cash flow from operating, investing, and financing activities.

### 3.2 Section Breakdown  

| Activity | Typical Items | Effect on Cash |
|----------|---------------|----------------|
| **Operating** | Net profit, changes in receivables, payables, inventory, depreciation | Core business cash generation |
| **Investing** | Purchase of equipment, sale of assets | Usually a cash outflow |
| **Financing** | Loan draws, repayments, shareholder withdrawals | Reflects financing decisions |

The **Net Cash Flow** at the bottom tells you the change in cash balance over the selected period. This number should reconcile with the **Bank Account** balances you reviewed in Chapter 7.

### 3.3 Using the Report for Decision‑Making  

- **Positive Operating Cash Flow**: Indicates the business can fund its day‑to‑day operations without borrowing.  
- **Negative Investing Cash Flow**: May be a good sign if you’re purchasing new equipment to grow.  
- **Large Financing Outflows**: Could signal loan repayments that need monitoring.

### 3.4 Customising and Exporting  

- **Filters**: Exclude certain tracking categories if you want a cleaner view.  
- **Export**: Same steps as the Balance Sheet—PDF for presentation, Excel for deeper analysis (e.g., building a cash‑flow forecast).

## 4. Aged Receivables & Payables Reports  

These reports help you manage **working capital** by showing which invoices are overdue and by how many days.

### 4.1 Why “Aged” Matters  

- **Aged Receivables**: Shows money owed **to** you. Long overdue invoices may need follow‑up or a credit policy review.  
- **Aged Payables**: Shows money you owe **to** suppliers. Keeping track prevents late‑payment penalties and maintains good supplier relationships.

### 4.2 Running the Aged Receivables Report  

1. **Reports** → **Aged Receivables**.  
2. Choose a **date** (usually today).  
3. Set the **age brackets** (e.g., 0‑30, 31‑60, 61‑90, >90 days). Xero defaults to these intervals, but you can edit them under **Settings** → **Aged Receivables Settings** if your business prefers different cut‑offs.

The report lists each customer, the total amount outstanding, and the amount in each age bucket.

### 4.3 Running the Aged Payables Report

# Chapter 10: 10. Year‑End Tasks and Tax Preparation

## A Real‑World Year‑End Scenario  

Emma runs a boutique graphic‑design studio called **Pixel & Print**. Her fiscal year ends on 30 June, and she has just received a reminder from her accountant: “All books must be closed and the trial balance ready for the tax return by 15 July.”  
Emma knows she has been reconciling her bank feed every month (Chapter 7) and that every invoice, bill, and expense claim is already entered (Chapters 5 & 6). What she hasn’t done yet is the **final reconciliation**, **locking the financial year**, and **producing the reports her accountant needs**. The steps below walk Emma—and any beginner—through exactly that process inside Xero.

---

## 1. Year‑End Preparation Checklist  

Before touching the lock date, make sure the books are truly “finished”. Use this checklist inside Xero; each item should be **green‑checked** before moving on.

| ✅ Checklist Item | Why It Matters |
|-------------------|----------------|
| **All bank feeds are up to date** – last transaction posted on or before the final day of the year. | Guarantees the cash balance reflects reality. |
| **All invoices and credit notes are posted** – no draft or awaiting approval items. | Prevents revenue from being omitted. |
| **All supplier bills and expense claims are entered** – including any year‑end accruals. | Ensures expenses are matched to the correct period. |
| **Outstanding payments & receipts are reviewed** – decide whether to leave them as open items or record an accrual. | Avoids surprise adjustments after the lock. |
| **Fixed‑asset register is current** – depreciation for the year is posted (Chapter 8). | Affects profit and tax depreciation schedules. |
| **Tax codes are correct** – GST/VAT, PAYE, and other tax codes have been applied to each transaction. | Critical for accurate tax reports. |
| **Reconcile any “Unreconciled” items** – use the **Bank Reconciliation** screen (Chapter 7). | Leaves no stray amounts that could throw off the trial balance. |
| **Review the Profit & Loss and Balance Sheet** – run a quick report (Chapter 9) to spot anomalies. | Early detection of data entry errors. |

When every checkbox is ticked, you are ready for the final steps.

---

## 2. Performing the Final Reconciliation  

### 2.1 Run a Last‑Minute Bank Reconciliation  

1. **Navigate to** **Accounting > Bank accounts**.  
2. Click **Reconcile** on the bank account that closes on the fiscal year‑end date.  
3. **Filter** the view to show transactions **up to 30 June** (or your year‑end).  
4. For each **unreconciled** line:  
   - If the transaction is genuine, click **Match** with the corresponding bank line.  
   - If the transaction is a **mistake** (e.g., duplicate entry), open the transaction and either **Delete** or **Void** it.  
5. Once the list is empty, Xero will display **“All items reconciled”** for that period.

> **Tip:** If you have a few outstanding supplier bills that haven’t been paid, you can **record an accrual** (a journal entry) so the expense appears in the current year. See Chapter 8 for creating a journal.

### 2.2 Lock the Financial Year  

Locking prevents anyone from posting transactions dated before the lock date, which safeguards the integrity of the year‑end figures.

1. **Settings > Financial Settings** (gear icon → **Advanced** → **Financial Settings**).  
2. Locate the **“Lock Dates”** section.  
3. Enter the **last day of the financial year** (e.g., **30 June 2026**) in the **“Lock Date”** field.  
4. Click **Save**. Xero will show a confirmation banner: *“Your organization is now locked to 30 June 2026.”*  

> **What the lock does:**  
> - No new transactions can be dated **before** 30 June 2026.  
> - Existing transactions can still be **edited**, but the date cannot be moved to an earlier period.  

If your accountant needs a **pre‑lock review**, set the lock date a few days later, run the reports, and then lock it for real once the accountant signs off.

---

## 3. Generating a Trial Balance and Supporting Tax Schedules  

### 3.1 The Trial Balance Explained  

A **trial balance** lists every ledger account with its ending **debit** or **credit** balance. In a double‑entry system, total debits must equal total credits—this is the first check that the books are mathematically sound.

### 3.2 Exporting the Trial Balance  

1. **Accounting > Reports** → **Trial Balance**.  
2. Set the **date range** to cover the whole financial year (e.g., **01 July 2025 – 30 June 2026**).  
3. Choose **“Export”** → **Excel** (or CSV).  
4. Save the file with a clear name, e.g., `PixelAndPrint_TB_2025-26.xlsx`.  

The exported file will contain columns for **Account Code**, **Account Name**, **Debit**, **Credit**, and **Balance**. This is the core document your accountant will use to verify the books.

### 3.3 Common Supporting Schedules  

| Schedule | Xero Report | Typical Use |
|----------|-------------|-------------|
| **GST/VAT Return** | **Business > VAT Return** (or **GST Return** in countries using GST) | Summarises taxable sales, purchases, and the net GST payable. |
| **PAYE / Payroll Summary** | **Payroll > Reports > Payroll Summary** | Shows employee earnings, tax withheld, and superannuation contributions. |
| **Depreciation Schedule** | **Accounting > Fixed assets** → **Depreciation Summary** | Lists each asset, its cost, accumulated depreciation, and net book value. |
| **Expense Breakdown** | **Reports > Expense Claims** or **Profit & Loss** with **“Detail”** view | Provides a line‑item view of expenses for tax deductions. |

**How to export each schedule:**  

- Open the report.  
- Adjust the date filter to the fiscal year.  
- Click **Export** → **PDF** (for a read‑only version) or **Excel** (for further manipulation).  

### 3.4 Creating a Custom Tax Pack (Optional)  

If your accountant prefers a single file containing all required schedules:

1. Go to **Accounting > Reports** → **Custom Reports**.  
2. Click **“+ New Custom Report”**.  
3. Add the **Trial Balance**, **GST Return**, **Depreciation Summary**, and any other needed reports as separate tabs.  
4. Save and **Export** the whole pack as a PDF.  

This saves time and reduces the chance of missing a required document.

---

## 4. Sharing the Year‑End Data with Your Accountant  

Xero makes collaboration secure and straightforward. Choose the method that matches your accountant’s workflow.

### 4.1 Invite the Accountant as a User  

1. **Settings > General Settings** → **Users**.  
2. Click **“Invite a User”**.  
3. Enter the accountant’s **email address**.  
4. Select the **role** **“Advisor”** (or **“Read‑Only”** if you only want them to view).  
5. Tick the **“Enable access to all reports”** box.  
6. Click **Send Invite**.  

The accountant receives a secure link to create a Xero login (or link to an existing one). Once accepted, they can:

- View all reports, including the trial balance and tax schedules.  
- Run additional reports if needed.  
- Add adjusting journal entries (if you grant them edit rights).  

> **Best practice:** Use a **distinct email** for the accountant (e.g., `accountant@pixelandprint.com`) to keep audit trails clean.

### 4.2 Export and Send Files Directly  

If the accountant prefers files:

1. Export each required report as **PDF** or **Excel** (see Section 3).  
2. Compress the files into a **ZIP** folder named `PixelAndPrint_YearEnd_2025-26.zip`.  
3. **Encrypt** the ZIP with a strong password (e.g., using 7‑Zip).  
4. Email the encrypted ZIP **and** send the password via a **different channel** (e.g., SMS or a phone call).  

### 4.3 Using Xero’s “File > Share” Feature  

Xero also offers a **“Share Document”** button on many reports:

- Click **Share** → **“Create shareable link”**.  
- Set an **expiration date** (e.g., 7 days).  
- Copy the link and send it to the accountant.  

This method avoids attachments and keeps the latest version always available.
